claims.text: Adding a moderate concentration of a transition metal such as Fe or Ni improves glass-forming ability in a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy.
Adding a moderate concentration of a transition metal such as Fe or Ni improves the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
Fe or Ni has a high mixing enthalpy with phosphorus.
A transition-metal concentration of 5–15 at% is moderate and suitable for the proposed intervention.
The proposed effect is expected under rapid-quenching or melt-spinning conditions.
Adding the transition metal enhances atomic-size mismatch in the alloy.
Adding the transition metal increases the negative mixing enthalpy associated with phosphorus–transition-metal interactions.
Enhanced size mismatch and negative mixing enthalpy increase topological and chemical disorder.
Transition-metal–phosphorus interactions increase the energy barrier for crystallization.
Frustration of atomic rearrangement promotes a more stable amorphous structure.
The modified alloy will have a higher critical cooling rate for glass formation than the baseline.
A higher critical cooling rate represents easier glass formation.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the baseline.
Transition-metal concentrations above 20 at% may cause phase separation.
Transition-metal concentrations above 20 at% may cause formation of crystalline intermetallics.
Phase separation or crystalline-intermetallic formation would reduce glass-forming ability and amorphous-state stability.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome specifies a higher critical cooling rate, whereas the falsification rule treats a lower critical cooling rate as the expected improvement.

The field equates a higher critical cooling rate with easier glass formation. Ordinarily, easier glass formation corresponds to a lower required critical cooling rate, making the stated metric direction inconsistent with its interpretation.
